fact: The same color looks different next to different neighbors. A gray looks lighter on a dark ground than on a light one.
product_use: Judge a color only on the real surface it will sit on.
check: Preview every swatch on the actual background and raised surface.

fact: Vivid colors look brighter than a gray with the same luminance (the Helmholtz-Kohlrausch effect).
product_use: A saturated accent can feel louder than its contrast number says. Do not separate two items by equal luminance alone.
check: Put a vivid accent next to a gray of equal lightness and look.

fact: Adding white to a hue shifts the hue you see (the Abney effect). Blue tints drift toward purple.
product_use: Check the lightest steps of a ramp for hue drift, most of all for blue.
check: Compare step 100 and step 500 by eye on a white surface.

fact: Perceived hue changes with luminance (the Bezold-Brucke effect).
product_use: A dark and a light step of one ramp can read as slightly different hues. Bend the hue a little across a long ramp.
check: View a full ramp as one strip.

fact: In dim light the eye gets more sensitive to blue and less to red (the Purkinje shift).
product_use: Night modes and car cabins make red fade. Never let red alone carry a critical state in a dim setting.
check: Test night and car themes in a dark room.

fact: The eye adapts to its surroundings. A large white page glows in a dark room.
product_use: Offer a dark mode, and avoid large pure white areas in it.
check: Check the dark theme at low screen brightness.

fact: Equal hue steps do not look equal. Greens and cyans cover a wide range, reds and blues a narrow one.
product_use: Do not split 360 degrees evenly to make categories. Pick by distance in OKLab, as `theme.py scale` does.
check: Look at the categorical scale as swatches.

fact: Yellow cannot get dark. At low lightness it turns olive or brown.
product_use: Use amber or yellow as a fill with dark text on it, not as text on white.
check: Measure warning text on its ground.

fact: Pure blue has very low luminance.
product_use: Blue text on a dark ground fails early. Move blue steps lighter in dark mode.
check: Measure the link color in both modes.

fact: About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have a red-green color deficiency.
product_use: Never use red against green as the only signal.
check: Run the CVD simulation in `theme.py build` and read its notes.

fact: Blue-yellow deficiency is rare but real. Some blue and yellow pairs collapse for those users.
product_use: Include the tritan view when you check a categorical scale.
check: `theme.py scale` checks protan, deutan and tritan.

fact: Legibility comes from lightness difference. Hue difference does not make text readable.
product_use: Judge text by contrast ratio, not by how different the hues look.
check: Convert the screen to grayscale and read it.

fact: sRGB is the default web gamut. Display P3 holds more saturated colors on screens that support it.
product_use: Define colors in sRGB first. Add P3 as an upgrade with a fallback.
check: Wrap P3 values in `@media (color-gamut: p3)`.

fact: HSL lightness is not perceptual. Yellow and blue at the same HSL lightness look very different in brightness.
product_use: Do not build ramps in HSL.
check: Compare the OKLCH lightness of two ramps that share an HSL lightness.

fact: OKLab and OKLCH keep lightness and hue closer to what people see, so ramps come out even.
product_use: Build ramps and mixes in OKLCH.
check: Print the lightness of each ramp step and look for even gaps.

fact: Plain CIE LCH bends blue toward purple when you change lightness. OKLab fixes most of that.
product_use: If a tool uses CIE LCH, check blue steps by eye.
check: View a blue ramp as a strip.

fact: Not every OKLCH triple fits inside sRGB. High chroma at very light or very dark values is out of range.
product_use: Lower chroma and keep lightness and hue. Never lower lightness to fit.
check: Use `oklch_to_hex`, which clamps chroma.

fact: Mixing sRGB values directly gives dark, muddy midpoints.
product_use: Mix tints, shades and gradients in OKLab or in linear light.
check: Run `theme.py mix` and compare spaces.

fact: The space of a gradient changes how it looks. Complementary colors mixed in sRGB pass through gray. In OKLCH they pass through other hues.
product_use: Pick the space by intent: OKLab for calm blends, OKLCH for a hue sweep.
check: Preview the gradient both ways.

fact: A translucent color has no contrast of its own. The result depends on what is behind it.
product_use: Measure the composite over the real ground, in each mode.
check: Use `theme.py contrast`, which composites alpha.

fact: Out-of-gamut or HDR values get clipped on screens that cannot show them.
product_use: Always ship an sRGB fallback.
check: Test on a standard display.

fact: Lightness describes a surface against white. Brightness describes how much light a screen gives off.
product_use: Use lightness for ramps. Remember that screen brightness settings can wash out low contrast outdoors.
check: Check contrast with the screen at low brightness.

fact: Chroma is colorfulness at a given lightness. HSL saturation is not comparable across hues.
product_use: To calm a palette, lower chroma. Do not lower HSL saturation.
check: Compare a calm and a lively palette by chroma.

fact: The WCAG ratio uses relative luminance, not lightness.
product_use: A pair can look fine and still fail. Compute the ratio.
check: Run the essential pairs.

fact: WCAG 2 ratios treat light-on-dark and dark-on-light the same. APCA models the difference.
product_use: Use WCAG as the gate and APCA as advice, especially in dark mode.
check: Read the Lc column in `report.md`.

fact: Warm and cool are relative. Green and violet change temperature with their neighbors.
product_use: Judge temperature by the whole palette. Use the neutral temperature knob.
check: Try cool, as built and warm in `live.html`.

fact: The idea that warm colors advance and cool ones recede is weak and depends on context.
product_use: Do not build depth on it. Use lightness and contrast.
check: Test with real content.

fact: The tint of the neutrals changes the mood of a screen more than the accent does.
product_use: Tint neutrals slightly toward the brand hue or toward the wanted temperature.
check: Compare two neutral tints with the same accent.

fact: Screens add light. Red light plus green light gives yellow. Paint subtracts light.
product_use: Do not trust paint intuition in RGB. Blue plus yellow is not green on a screen.
check: Run `theme.py mix` on blue and yellow.

fact: The red-yellow-blue wheel is a teaching tool. Complements differ by color model.
product_use: Compute harmonies as hue angles in OKLCH and check by eye.
check: Look at the harmony as swatches.

fact: A tint adds white and lowers chroma. A shade adds black and lowers lightness. A tone adds gray and does both.
product_use: Define ramps by lightness and chroma targets, not by adding white or black.
check: Print L and C for each step.

fact: Print inks (CMYK) cannot show some bright blues, greens and oranges that a screen can.
product_use: Ask about print early and check brand colors in CMYK.
check: Ask the printer for a proof.

fact: A spot ink such as a Pantone color is a mixed ink, not a conversion of an RGB value.
product_use: Record the spot name and a screen hex, and say which one is the master.
check: Keep both in the brand sheet.

fact: Paper changes the color. Uncoated stock looks duller than coated stock.
product_use: Proof on the real paper.
check: Compare a printed swatch with the screen.

fact: The same hex looks different across devices. Screens are backlit and paper is reflective.
product_use: Set expectations early and test on the target devices.
check: Check on one phone, one laptop and one external display.

fact: Color meaning depends on region. Red can mean luck or danger. White can mean purity or mourning.
product_use: Use `data/locale-color-notes.csv` when the audience is regional.
check: Ask a local reviewer.

fact: For states, convention beats invention: red for error, green for success, amber for warning, blue for information.
product_use: Keep the conventions. Add an icon or a word so color is never alone.
check: Check each state with color removed.

fact: In some markets gain is red and loss is green.
product_use: Make gain and loss per-locale tokens.
check: Review the finance screens with a local user.

fact: A known brand hue is part of recognition.
product_use: Treat a confirmed brand color as fixed. Move other colors around it.
check: Ask which colors are confirmed.

fact: People can tell about six colors apart in a legend. Beyond that they need labels.
product_use: Cap a guaranteed categorical scale at 6. Label directly past that.
check: `theme.py scale categorical --n 8` reports the closest pair.

fact: In a sequential scale, lightness carries the order. The hue should change little.
product_use: Move lightness in even steps and bend hue a few degrees at most.
check: Check the smallest lightness step.

fact: A diverging scale needs a real midpoint, such as zero or a target.
product_use: Mirror the lightness on both sides of a neutral middle.
check: Convert the scale to grayscale. It should be symmetric.

fact: Touching marks blend in the eye.
product_use: Separate them with a 1 to 2 px stroke in the ground color.
check: Zoom on a stacked bar.

fact: Red against green for good against bad fails for many people.
product_use: Add an icon, a sign or a position cue.
check: View the chart in the deutan simulation.

fact: Color is a weak way to show exact values. Direct labels beat a legend.
product_use: Label marks. Use color to group, not to measure.
check: Remove the legend and see if the chart still reads.

fact: UI parts that carry meaning (input borders, icons, focus rings) need 3:1 against their neighbor.
product_use: Measure borders and focus rings, not only text.
check: Run the essential pairs.

fact: Normal text needs 4.5:1. Large text needs 3:1 (24 px, or 18.66 px bold).
product_use: Use 4.5:1 unless the text is clearly large.
check: Measure every text role.

fact: Forced colors modes replace your colors with system colors.
product_use: Keep borders and use system color keywords where it matters.
check: Test with forced colors on.

fact: Color alone fails users who cannot tell the colors apart.
product_use: Add an icon, a label or a shape to every color signal.
check: Run the grayscale and CVD checks.

fact: Phones offer an increased contrast setting that people turn on for a reason.
product_use: Offer a high contrast mode or stronger borders and text.
check: Test with the setting on.
